hints: Look for a carbon with four single bonds to four different groups, ignore all $C=C$ carbons and $CH_2$ and $C(CH_3)_2$ carbons.
walkthrough:
Apply the test for chirality**
Picture yourself checking each carbon one by one. A chiral centre must be $sp^3$, so it has four single bonds, and all four attached groups must be different. Any carbon in a $C=C$ double bond can be ruled out straight away, and any $CH_2$ or $C(CH_3)_2$ carbon has two identical $H$ or two identical $CH_3$ groups so it cannot be chiral.

Find the only carbon that passes**
In abscisic acid the only carbon with four different single bonds is the ring carbon carrying the $OH$ group. It is bonded to $OH$, to the side chain $-CH=CH-$, to the ring $C(CH_3)_2$ side and to the ring $C(CH_3)=$ side. Label that carbon with an asterisk. No other carbon qualifies.
Final answer: The chiral centre is the tertiary alcohol carbon in the ring, the $C$ bonded to $OH$ and to the side chain.

hints: Compare $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}_{4}$ with the product and think what change adds two $H$ atoms but keeps all four $O$ atoms, such as ketone to alcohol reduction.
walkthrough:
See what type of reduction keeps oxygen**
Think about what happens when a ketone $C=O$ is reduced to a secondary alcohol $CH-OH$. You add one $H$ to the carbon and one $H$ to the oxygen, so the net change is $+2[H]$ and the number of $O$ atoms does not change. That is exactly the reaction of $NaBH_4$ with the ring ketone.

Add the hydrogens to the formula**
Start from abscisic acid, $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}_{4}$. Add two $H$ atoms: $20 + 2 = 22$. Carbon and oxygen are unchanged, giving $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{4}$.

hints: Focus on cleavage of the trisubstituted $C=C$ in the six membered ring while retaining the gem-dimethyl group, the tertiary $OH$, the original ketone and the side chain carboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
Picture oxidative opening of the ring alkene**
Keep the picture of hot concentrated acidified $KMnO_4$ in mind. It breaks each $C=C$ completely and turns each alkene carbon into a carbonyl, then into a carboxylic acid if it has a $H$ to oxidise further. For the largest fragment, look at what happens when the endocyclic $C=C$ is cut open.

Track every group that survives**
The $C(CH_3)_2$ part stays as two $CH_3$ groups, the tertiary $C-OH$ stays intact, the ring $C=O$ stays as a ketone $O$, the ring $CH_3$ on the double bond becomes part of a new $CH_3-C=O$ ketone, and the $CH$ of the double bond becomes a new $COOH$. Together with the unchanged side chain $-CH=CH-C(CH_3)=CH-COOH$ you get a hydroxy keto diacid containing $CH_3$, $CH_3$, $COOH$, $OH$, $O$, $CH_3$, $O$ and $COOH$ groups.

Final answer: Largest product is the ring opened keto diacid alcohol: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{side chain})-\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ where side chain = $-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})=\text{CH}-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ retained.

hints: Think which one carbon fragment can be produced when an alkene carbon bearing $H$ or a terminal acid group is fully oxidised.
Recall the specific term used for $C=C$ bond breaking by hot acidified manganate(VII) that goes beyond aldehyde to $CO_2$.
walkthrough:
Spot where a single carbon is lost**
When the side chain $C=C$ bonds are cleaved, some alkene carbons carry only $H$ plus the double bond, for example the $=CH-CO_2H$ end. Under mild conditions this would give an aldehyde $O=CH-$, but hot concentrated $MnO_4^-$ is a very powerful oxidiser.

Explain the full oxidation to carbon dioxide**
That aldehyde intermediate is oxidised further to a carboxylic acid and then oxidatively decarboxylated under the vigorous conditions. The one carbon fragment is therefore fully oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$, which is why $\text{CO}_{2}$ is the product with the smallest molecular mass. The key term is oxidation by oxidative cleavage.
Final answer: $\text{CO}_{2}$ formed by oxidation / oxidative cleavage of the alkene.

hints: Look at the $\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})=\text{CH}-$ unit in the side chain and think what three carbon keto acid remains when that double bond is cut and the methyl bearing carbon becomes a ketone.
walkthrough:
Cut the side chain methyl substituted double bond**
Focus on the $-C(CH_3)=CH-COOH$ end. Oxidative cleavage splits the $C=C$. The carbon carrying the $CH_3$ has no $H$, so it stops at the ketone stage, giving $CH_3-C=O-$. The neighbouring $CH$ carbon is oxidised through to acid.

Rejoin the pieces**
Joining the acetyl piece $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$ directly to the new acid $-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCO}_{2}\text{H}$. That is pyruvic acid, 2-oxopropanoic acid, the third cleavage product.
